<reason>A wins by sustaining the chicken-and-egg coordination case. Its phased rising-share design with pooling, banking, and paid expiring availability relief directly answers B's waiver-or-detention dilemma without collapsing into a cliff-edge mandate, while B mainly reasserts that any exemption nullifies bindingness. A also turns enforcement symmetrically: if carbon pricing can be collected at concentrated bunkering and port hubs, a fuel rule can be checked there too, leaving B's pricing alternative raising freight without guaranteeing fuel, engines, safety codes, or bunkering on schedule. B's food-price and feasibility pressure remains strong, but its interim-cost critique is weakened by A's adoption-time rebates and gradual phase-in, and its clipped closing adds an execution cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 A1 was decisive: phased shares, pooling, banking, and priced time-limited exemptions answer B's strongest question by preserving a bankable obligation while avoiding detained vessels, undercutting B's claim that flexibility necessarily destroys the mandate.</best_rebuttal>
